core: what a credit card is: a card that lets a person borrow money up to a set limit, to be paid back later (working definition, attributed to FTC/CFPB)
how the billing cycle works: statement, due date, and grace period, each named and explained in one line; grace period named as the period between the end of the billing cycle and the due date
the costs named generally: interest on carried balances, late fees, annual fees, cash-advance fees (interest is a sibling topic; named but not taught)
minimum payments: paying the minimum keeps the balance alive and growing, with an original example and the statement disclosure box
credit cards and credit history: responsible use builds a record (credit-scores is a sibling topic, referenced only)
debit versus credit: your money versus borrowed money (checking-accounts is a sibling topic)
the honest framing: a credit card is a tool with a trapdoor
supporting: credit limit: the most a cardholder is allowed to borrow on the card, shown on the statement
late-payment timing: a payment is generally on time if received by 5 p.m. on the due date, or the next business day after a weekend or holiday
grace periods are common but not guaranteed: issuers are not required to offer one, though most do on purchases
the required disclosure box: issuers must show how long the current balance takes to clear if only the minimum is paid
lost or stolen card protections: reporting a lost or stolen card before it is used generally means the cardholder is not responsible for unauthorized charges (referenced, not a focus)

claims.claim: A credit card is a card that lets a person borrow money up to a set limit and pay it back later; the card issuer pays the merchant, and the cardholder owes that amount until the bill is paid.
A credit limit is the most the cardholder is allowed to borrow on the card, as shown on the monthly statement.
A billing cycle is the period a credit card statement covers, usually about a month; the statement is the monthly record of purchases, payments, fees, and the balance owed, and it names the due date.

A grace period is the time between the end of a billing cycle and the payment due date, during which interest may not be charged as long as the balance is paid in full by the due date; issuers are not required to offer one, but most do on purchases.

A payment is generally considered late if it is not received by 5 p.m. on the due date, or by the next business day when the due date falls on a weekend or holiday, and late payment can trigger a late fee.

The main costs of a credit card, named generally, are interest on carried (unpaid) balances, late fees, annual fees, and cash-advance fees; issuers may also charge other fees such as balance-transfer and over-limit fees.

If the full statement balance is not paid by the due date, the unpaid part carries into the next billing cycle and the issuer charges interest on it; the mechanics of interest are left to the sibling topic interest.

The minimum payment is the smallest amount that keeps the account in good standing; paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance to carry and accrue interest, and it can take years to pay off the balance that way.
Card issuers are required to show on each statement how long it would take to pay off the current balance if no new purchases were made and only the minimum payment were made.

Using a credit card responsibly, especially paying on time, helps build a good credit history; lenders use that history to decide whether to do business with a person and what to charge, and negative items such as missed payments make credit harder and more expensive to get.

Debit cards and prepaid cards spend money the person already has, while credit cards are a way to borrow money; with a debit card the purchase is drawn from the linked account, and with a credit card the purchase becomes an amount owed to the issuer.

A credit card is a tool with a trapdoor: used well (full payment by the due date, costs known, balance watched) it is convenient and builds a record; used badly (minimum payments only, fees ignored) the balance can grow for years — an interpretive framing consistent with the CFPB and FTC sources.

conflictingEvidence: Grace periods are not universal: CFPB and FTC both state that issuers are not required to give a grace period, though most do on purchases; the lesson presents the grace period as the common arrangement and notes explicitly that it is not guaranteed.

Fee amounts and structures vary by issuer and by card; neither CFPB nor FTC states universal dollar figures, so the lesson names the fee types generally (interest on carried balances, late fees, annual fees, cash-advance fees) without quoting amounts as universal.

Minimum-payment payoff times depend on the balance, the rate, and the issuer's formula; the lesson's example uses clearly illustrative figures and points readers to the disclosure box on their own statement for the actual numbers.

The old ask-cfpb page 'What is a credit card?' (en-510) returns 404; the working definition is supported instead by the live FTC comparing-cards article, the live CFPB debit-vs-credit answer (en-433), and the CFPB credit-cards hub.

sourceRecords.title: Credit cards (CFPB consumer-tools hub)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Frames credit cards as borrowing ('Your interest rate is what you pay for borrowing money'), lists key terms including grace period, and covers protections such as reporting a lost or stolen card before it is used. Supports the borrowing framing and the named mechanics.

sourceRecords.title: What is a grace period for a credit card?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Defines the grace period as the period between the end of a billing cycle and the date the payment is due, during which interest may not be charged if the balance is paid in full by the due date; states issuers are not required to give one but most credit cards provide a grace period on purchases.

sourceRecords.title: A box on my credit card bill says that I will pay off the balance in three years if I pay a certain amount. What does that mean?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Issuers must disclose on each statement how long the current balance takes to clear if only the minimum is paid and how much would clear it in 36 months; paying only the minimum can take years to pay off a card. Supports the minimum-payment honest note and the statement disclosure box.

sourceRecords.title: How are prepaid cards, debit cards, and credit cards different?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. States the your-money-versus-borrowed-money line: prepaid and debit cards spend money you already have, credit cards are ways to borrow money; borrowing must be repaid by the payment due date, paying late generally means a late fee, and paying less than the full amount means paying interest.

sourceRecords.title: Why do I need a credit history?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. A credit history helps a person get housing, bank accounts, credit cards, and loans, and affects how much interest is paid; negative items such as missed payments and high balances make credit harder and more expensive to get. Supports the credit-history connection.

sourceRecords.title: When is my credit card payment considered late?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. A payment is generally on time if received by 5 p.m. on the due date, or the next business day after a weekend or holiday; paying on time avoids late fees and, with a full balance, interest on purchases. Supports the due-date mechanics.

sourceRecords.title: Using Credit Cards and Disputing Charges
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Working definition: 'With a credit card, you borrow money to buy something now. Later you pay back the money, usually with interest.' Names the grace period as the time between the end of the billing period and when the payment is due; paying only the minimum means paying interest on the rest and makes credit more expensive; on-time payments build credit history.

sourceRecords.title: Comparing Credit, Charge, Secured Credit, Debit, or Prepaid Cards
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. The monthly statement shows interest paid and the credit limit, 'the most you're allowed to borrow on the card'; fees named include annual fees, cash advances, balance transfers, over-limit charges, and late fees; carrying a balance means interest on the unpaid balance; paying bills on time helps build a good credit history.
